opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's because that paper was the first time I felt like I actually figured out how to tell a story with the science instead of just reporting results.

With the original lottery ticket paper, a lot of the writing was me trying to convince people the phenomenon was real. It was a bit breathless. There were lots of experiments and figures, and I was throwing everything at the wall. The linear mode connectivity paper was different. We had a fairly simple question: if you train two copies of a network from the same starting point, but with different SGD noise like different data orders, do they end up in the same linearly connected region of the loss landscape? Then we had a clean connection back to lottery tickets, which is that the subnetworks only seem to work once they become stable to that noise in this linear-connectivity sense.

What I'm proud of is that the paper is built around that one idea and doesn't wander. Every section has a job. We define the instability analysis carefully, show what it reveals about dense networks, and then show what it explains about sparse networks and why rewinding to an early iteration rather than to initialization matters at scale. I spent a lot of time cutting things. There were experiments I loved that just didn't serve the argument, and they went to the appendix or disappeared entirely.

I also tried hard to be precise about what we were and weren't claiming. In this field it's very easy to overclaim, to say "this is why neural networks work." I wanted the paper to be careful, to say "here is a phenomenon, here's exactly how we measured it, here's where it holds and where it doesn't." I think that restraint actually made the paper more persuasive.

So for me, it was a lesson that writing isn't a wrapper you put on the research at the end. Figuring out how to say something clearly forces you to figure out what you actually found. That paper is the one where I feel like the writing and the science really came together.

r001.rationale: He says the paper was the first time he felt he had figured out how to tell a story with the science, and describes building it around one clear idea and cutting material that did not serve the argument. This communicates pride in making the research story clear and comprehensible.

fable-5.1.text:
That paper was really the first time I felt like I'd written a paper rather than just assembled one. With the original lottery ticket work, the ideas were there but the writing was, honestly, a bit of a mess. I was learning how to do this. With the linear mode connectivity paper, I sat down with the goal of making the paper something people would actually enjoy reading.

A few things I'm proud of. First, we had a genuinely clean conceptual story: this notion of stability to SGD noise, which you can test by training two copies of a network from the same point with different data orders and seeing whether they end up in the same linearly connected basin. And then the observation that this property lines up almost exactly with when lottery ticket rewinding starts to work. That's a nice, tight idea, and I think the writing lets it breathe. We tried to say one thing clearly rather than ten things halfway.

Second, I worked hard on the figures and on making sure each one had a single message. I have a rule for myself now that if you can read only the figure captions and the section headings, you should still be able to follow the paper. I think that one mostly passes the test.

And third, I tried to be honest about what we didn't know. There's a lot of hedging in deep learning papers that's really just vagueness dressed up as caution. I wanted to say precisely what we observed, precisely where we observed it, and precisely which questions were still open. That kind of clarity is harder than it sounds, because you have to actually understand your own results well enough to draw those lines. Writing it forced me to understand the work better, and I think that's the mark of a paper you can be proud of.

r001.rationale: He says he aimed to make the paper something people would enjoy reading, presents its conceptual story clearly, and describes making figures and sections easy to follow. This communicates pride in making the research story comprehensible.

astra-6.text:
I’m proud of it because we found a clear story for a pretty complicated set of experiments. The lottery ticket hypothesis asks whether you can find a small subnetwork that trains successfully in isolation. But there was this puzzle: pruning at initialization didn’t work reliably for larger networks, while letting the network train for a little while before rewinding did. Why should that little bit of training matter so much?

Linear mode connectivity gave us a way to investigate that. Take two copies of a network at the same point in training, train them with different randomness, and then look at the loss along the straight line between their final weights. We found a connection between when those solutions became connected by a low-loss path and when the pruned subnetworks started training successfully.

The writing puts that question and the evidence front and center. It takes the reader through why we did each experiment and what we learned, without making the result sound like we’d explained everything. That’s hard to get right, and I’m really happy with how we did it.

r001.rationale: He says they found a clear story for a complicated set of experiments and describes how the writing guides readers through the question, experiments, and findings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we did a good job of telling the story of how we came to understand the result. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, we had this observation that you could find these small subnetworks that trained well, but we didn’t really understand why training them from initialization could be so fragile, or why rewinding them a little bit into training helped so much.

Linear mode connectivity gave us a way to ask a more precise question: if you train the same network twice with different randomness, do the solutions end up connected by a straight line with low loss? And how does that change as you move through those first few iterations of training?

What I’m proud of in the writing is that we tried to make that progression clear—here’s the puzzle, here’s a tool for investigating it, and here’s what the evidence does and doesn’t tell us. There’s a temptation to make a paper sound like you understood everything from the beginning. I think this one does a nice job of bringing the reader along as the understanding develops.

r001.rationale: He says they made the research progression clear and brought readers along as their understanding developed, identifying clear storytelling as what he is proud of in the writing.
